Skip `.env*` and environment values under 8 characters, so `PORT=3000` does not redact every 3000.

sections.title: Usage records
sections.summary: Reads Codex rollouts into per-call usage records (codexUsageOf), stores them idempotently in a new usage_calls table alongside session allocations and subagent links, and computes each task's usage total over distinct, share-weighted sessions (taskUsageOf), surfaced on TraceTask.usage.

requirements.text: `cairn session put --task <task> --id <session> --format codex` stores a Codex rollout read from stdin the same way it stores a Claude Code log: redacted, under the session ID.
A Codex session must not enter `cairn.db` by any path other than explicit linking with `cairn session put`.
`codexUsageOf(log)` is a pure function.

Before `codexUsageOf` is written, a real Codex rollout on the machine is read and a trimmed copy is kept as the test fixture; the rollout field names the reader uses are checked against that fixture rather than assumed.
Rollout lines carrying the turn's context set the model and reasoning setting in effect; a change partway through a session applies from that line onward.
Token count lines are treated as cumulative totals, and each call's usage is the difference from the previous snapshot.
A token count snapshot equal to the previous one adds no usage.
A cumulative total lower than the previous one starts a new segment (as when a session resumes) and adds no negative usage.
Each usage record is `{ callKey, at, model, reasoning, input, cachedInput, output, reasoningTokens }`, where `callKey` is formed from the line's timestamp and the cumulative total.
Reasoning tokens are counted as part of output tokens, as Codex reports them.
A snapshot with no model in effect keeps `model: null`, and its cost stays unknown.
The planned model must never be substituted for a missing model on a usage record.
Rate-limit snapshots on token count lines go to the subscription allowance (spec.sessions.subscription-allowance), not to usage records.
A new migration creates the `usage_calls` and `allocations` tables and adds `parent_id` and `purpose` columns to `sessions`.
Usage calls are inserted with `on conflict do nothing`, so importing the same session twice changes nothing.
Usage is keyed by session, so linking two commits to one session counts its usage once.
`--parent <session>` links a subagent session to its parent, and a subagent's usage counts once, toward its parent's task.
`cairn session allocate <session> <task>=<share> ...` splits a shared session across tasks; each share must lie in (0, 1] and the shares must sum to at most 1.
Whatever part of a session is not allocated stays unassigned.
A session with no allocation goes wholly to its `task_id`.
A session that names no task and has no allocation is assigned to no task.

`taskUsageOf(task, sessions, calls, allocations)` is pure and takes each distinct session once — the task's own sessions, their subagents, and its review and conflict sessions — weighting each by its share.
Per-call usage is priced by `estimateOf` with dated rates, and the task total is exposed as `TraceTask.usage`.

sections.title: API-equivalent cost
sections.summary: Builds the pure function `estimateOf(calls, catalog)`. It prices each call in a session from the model catalog and returns an `Estimate`, labelled API-equivalent cost. The estimate is deterministic, works in integer micro-dollars, tracks which calls were priced, and records its rate sources, assumptions and excluded charges.

requirements.text: `estimateOf(calls, catalog)` must be pure and must return an `Estimate`.
Everywhere the estimate is shown, it must be labelled `API-equivalent cost`.
The estimate must never be presented as billed cost.
Each call must be priced with `priceOf(model, at)`.
Uncached input (input tokens minus cached input tokens) must be charged at the input rate.
Cached input must be charged at the cached rate.
Cache writes must be charged at the cache-write rate when they are reported.
Output must be charged at the output rate.
When the price entry has service-tier or long-context rates and the call matches them, those rates must apply.
Reasoning tokens are already counted in output and must not be charged a second time.
The reasoning level must not be used as a cost multiplier.
Arithmetic must be done in integer micro-dollars and summed in call order, so the same calls always give the same estimate.
Displayed estimates must be rounded to cents.
A call with no price or no model must be treated as unpriced, which makes the estimate partial, with `coverage.priced` less than `coverage.calls`.
When no call is priced, the estimate's `usd` must be `null`.
A price must never be guessed.
`sources` must list the source and effective date of each rate used.
`assumptions` must record the choices made while estimating, such as "cache writes not reported by Codex, so not charged".
`excluded` must name the charges the estimate cannot see, such as "tool charges (web search, file search)".

sections.title: Subscription allowance
sections.summary: Builds subscription accounting for sessions billed on a plan rather than per token. It stores Codex rate-limit snapshots and turns them into account use and per-session allowance consumption with `allowanceOf`. It also spreads a configured subscription fee across sessions with `allocationOf`. Billed cost stays `null` throughout.

requirements.text: A subscription attempt keeps `cost: null` for the cost metrics, and allowance and allocation are shown beside it as separate estimates.
The `exclusive` flag on a configured subscription defaults to false.
Codex's rate-limit snapshots, read by `codexUsageOf`, are stored in the `allowance_snapshots` table.
An allowance is identified as `<subscription id>:<window>`, one for each window the provider reports.
Separate allowance windows must never be merged.
No fixed token cap may be assumed for an allowance or derived from prices.
`allowanceOf(snapshots, sessions, subscriptions)` is a pure function.
Account use is each allowance's latest snapshot. It gives used and remaining percent and the time the snapshot was observed, and it is labelled `Account (all use)`.
A session's consumption is the change between its first and last snapshots in the same allowance with the same `resets_at`.
When a reset falls between a session's snapshots, the change is split at the reset, and no part of the consumption may be negative.
A fall in used percent within one window is treated as a missing snapshot.

Consumption is attributed to a session only when its subscription is `exclusive` and no other session in `cairn.db` using the same allowance overlaps it in time. Otherwise the session's share is `null` and the account change is shown as context.
Each allowance share carries the note `±1 point: Codex reports whole percents`.
`allocationOf(subscription, period, sessions)` is a pure function.
When a fee is configured, the period's budget is `amount × share`. It is spread over the period's sessions on that subscription in proportion to their API-equivalent estimates.
An allocation for a period that is still open is marked `provisional`.
The allocation is `null` when an included session has an unknown API-equivalent estimate or when the total of the estimates is zero.
The allocation states its method as `fee × share, in proportion to API-equivalent estimates, <n> sessions`.
The allocation is labelled `Allocated subscription cost` and is presented as neither a provider charge nor allowance consumed.
The allocated subscription cost must not set a cap.
Allowance and allocation data stay in `cairn.db` and in the private trace fields.

Each provider-reported window is its own allowance. Windows are never merged, and no fixed token cap is assumed or derived from prices.
A share of allowance consumption is claimed only for an `exclusive` subscription with no overlapping session on the same allowance. Without `exclusive`, no share is claimed.

decisions.text: A fall in used percent within one window is treated as a missing snapshot rather than as negative consumption.
The subscription fee is allocated across sessions in proportion to their API-equivalent estimates, and the allocation is neither a provider charge nor a cap.

sections.title: Notes
sections.summary: Adds notes and reviews anchored to link paths: a Note type and `notes` table, `cairn note add` and `cairn note resolve` commands, and server support that reads notes into the trace and attaches them to their sessions.

requirements.text: The contract must define a Note type with id, kind ("note" or "review"), author, markdown body, status ("open" or "resolved"), anchor (a link path), task, session, at and resolvedAt, and the Trace must gain a `notes` array of Note.
A new migration must add a `notes` table with the Note's columns.
A note must hang off the session ID when there is one.
A note must never hang off the commit.
`cairn note add --kind <kind> --author <author> [--session <id>] <link arguments>` must store a note.
`cairn note add` must read the note's body from stdin, or from `--body`.
`cairn note add` must build the anchor from the same arguments as `cairn link` using `stepsOfArgs`, and encode it with `LinkFromPath`.
A note's `task` must be the link's task step, or else the session's task.
`cairn note add` must print the stored note's ID and its link.
`cairn note add` must exit 1 when the link arguments name an unknown task.

sections.title: Orchestrator adapter
sections.summary: Lists what the existing orchestrator must do per task using only @cairn/contract/js and the CLI.

requirements.text: Read the manifest with `parseManifest`.

Take every task that is `pending` in `cairn status --json` whose dependencies are `done` or `landed`, and whose dependencies off its own chain are `landed`, and run them in parallel; how many run at once is the orchestrator's choice.

Work in the task's worktree (the repo's own checkout when null, otherwise `git worktree add ../<repo>-<worktree>` the first time), then `gt checkout` the parent branch, or `baseBranch` after `gt sync` when the task has no parent.
Call `appendEvent` with `running`.
Run the agent with a new session ID; its first commit is `gt create <branch> -m <message>` and later ones are `gt modify --commit -m <message>`, each message ending with the `formatTrailers` block.
Pipe the session log to `cairn session put`.
Call `appendEvent` with `failed`, or `blocked_on_human` when `humanGate.required`, and `done` otherwise.
A blocked task stops its chain until `cairn approve`.
The orchestrator uses only `@cairn/contract/js` and the CLI.
`gt submit --stack` opens or updates one pull request per task, and `gt sync` pulls baseBranch, deletes merged branches and restacks the rest.
Neither Cairn nor the orchestrator rebases a branch by hand; Graphite owns branches, restacking and pull requests.
Landing is read from git: a squash merge carries the task's trailers onto baseBranch.
No Graphite command runs with `--no-verify`; hooks gate every commit.

sections.title: Attempts and verification
sections.summary: Defines what the orchestrator adds to each task run: attempt metadata on the `running` event, a verify command run in the task's worktree that decides `done`, `blocked_on_human` or `failed` (with a failure kind), usage, cost and route on the final event, and session and usage recording through the cairn CLI. AGENTS.md documents these fields for adapter writers.

requirements.text: The `running` event the orchestrator emits for a task carries `session`, `harness`, `model`, `reasoning` and `attempt`.
A retry attempt keeps the same model and reasoning as the attempt before it.
An escalation attempt raises either the model or the reasoning, or hands the task to a person.
An attempt that repairs a task after review is recorded as attempt `repair`.
When the agent stops, the orchestrator runs `config.verify.command` in the task's worktree.
`config.verify.command` defaults to `pnpm check`, which runs the tests the spec sections name and the repo's checks.
A verify command exit code of 0 gives the task `done`, or `blocked_on_human` when the task is gated.
Any non-zero verify command exit gives the task `failed` with `failure: "checks"`.
An attempt where the agent gives up fails with failure `agent`.
An attempt that ends in a runner, provider or network error fails with failure `infra`.
An attempt that fails because a dependency turns out to be wrong fails with failure `upstream`.
The adapter must not add its own detector for changes to checks, lint rules and tests an attempt did not write; the repo's hooks catch those.
The `done` or `failed` event carries `usage`, `cost` and `route`.
A run on a subscription reports `cost: null` and route `subscription`.
The orchestrator sends the attempt's session to `cairn session put`, and passes the provider's raw usage report to `--usage` when the provider gave one.
A review or conflict resolution session on a task is recorded as a usage event carrying its `purpose`.
The orchestrator must not start again a task that has `terminal: true` in `cairn status --json`.
`AGENTS.md` lists the event fields above for anyone writing an adapter.

sections.title: Conflict-aware running
sections.summary: Adds conflict-aware scheduling: a pure `scheduleOf` that orders ready tasks by conflict risk against running tasks, detects overlapping hunks between running tasks, and orders stack landing. It also covers the orchestrator behaviour (hold/release/notice/restack events, notices to agents, restacking on land) and how conflict events show in `cairn status` and the viewer timeline.

requirements.text: Conflict events (`ConflictEvent`, kind "conflict", with action hold, release, notice or restack) must join the `Event` union.
A held task must stay `pending`, and its hold event must name the task it waits on.
Once a task is running, `Git.changedFiles(branch)` must replace its planned files in `scoreOf`.

`Git.changedFiles(branch)` must return the files of the branch's commits plus the uncommitted changes in its worktree, finding the worktree with `git worktree list --porcelain` and reading changes with `git diff --name-only <merge-base>`.
`Git.patch(branch)` must return the same diff as `Git.changedFiles(branch)`, as hunks.
`scheduleOf(trace, scores, patches, config)` must be pure, and its result must go into `cairn status --json` as `Trace.schedule`.
`Schedule.ready` must list every task that can start, sorted by `hold`, then by the task's highest score against a running task, then by task ID.
A ready entry's `hold` must be set when its highest score against a running task is at or above `conflicts.high`.
The orchestrator must fill free agents from the top of `ready`, taking a `hold` task only when no task without `hold` is left.
When the orchestrator passes over a held task for another, it must write a `hold` event, and it must write a `release` event when the task the hold waits on lands.

`Schedule.notices` must hold one entry for each pair of running tasks whose hunks change overlapping lines of the same file on the base version of that file, with `first` set to whichever task's stack lands first.

`Schedule.landing` must hold, for each pair of stacks with a high score between their unfinished tasks, an order in which the stack with fewer unfinished tasks lands first, ties broken by fewer changed lines, then by the lower stack number.
`cairn status` must print each landing order in the form `land stack 12 before stack 9 (shares packages/core/src/lint.ts)`.
For each new notice, the orchestrator must write a `notice` event on both tasks.

For each new notice, the orchestrator must send `formatNotice(notice)` to both agents through the channel it gives briefs on, e.g. `t15 also changes packages/core/src/lint.ts lines 40–62. t12 lands first; restack onto it as soon as it lands.`
When a stack lands, the orchestrator must tell every running or waiting stack that scores against it to restack at once (`gt sync`).
On a restack, the orchestrator must write one `restack` event per stack, recording `conflicted` and the files git stopped on.
The orchestrator must not stop or reassign a running agent.
Conflict messages to agents must come only from the orchestrator.

The viewer's detail panel timeline must show a task's conflict events from its `events`, e.g. `held behind t12 (0.72, packages/core/src/lint.ts)`, `told: t12 lands first`, `restacked onto t12, conflicted in lint.ts`.

With one free agent and only held tasks ready, a held task starts.
Two running tasks with overlapping hunks give one notice naming both tasks and the file (acceptance criterion).

`ready` holds exactly the tasks that can start.
`landing` is the same whatever order the stacks come in.

decisions.text: A held task stays `pending` rather than getting a new status; the hold event names what it waits on.
For running tasks, live changed files from git replace planned files in scoring.
The orchestrator takes a held task when no task without `hold` is left, rather than leaving an agent idle.
decisions.why: So no agent sits idle only to avoid a risk.

decisions.text: When stacks conflict, the stack with fewer unfinished tasks lands first, then the one with fewer changed lines, then the lower stack number.
The orchestrator never stops or reassigns a running agent.
decisions.why: That is a person's call.

decisions.text: Messages come only from the orchestrator; delivery through the room and adapters for message boards are left for later (`prd.later`).

sections.title: `cairn link`
sections.summary: Builds the `cairn link` command, which turns ordered command-line tokens into viewer steps, checks them against the PRD, spec, manifest and git, and prints a viewer deep link encoded with `LinkFromPath`. It also sets the rule that agents and the orchestrator name places in PRs, gate notices and board posts with `cairn link`.

requirements.text: `cairn link` prints a link into the viewer.
`cairn link` builds the steps from its arguments in the order they are given and writes the path with `LinkFromPath`, so its output is the same path the viewer copies.
`stepsOfArgs(tokens, plan)` in `link-args.ts` reads the arguments left to right and is pure.
A token starting with `prd.` or `spec.` becomes a `section` step.
`--passage <text>` right after a section token turns that section step into a `passage` step, with the text collapsed the way a quote is.
A token that is a task ID in the manifest becomes a `task` step.
`--commit <sha>` becomes a `commit` step.
`--file <path>` becomes a `file` step. When it follows a `task` step, it first adds a `diff` step at the task's newest commit, read with `Git.log`.
`--line <n>` or `--line <n>-<m>` becomes a `lines` step on the new side. `--old` before it puts the lines on the old side.
`--stack <root>`, `--segment <root>`, `--turn <session>/<turn>` and `--note <id>` each become their own step.
The command declares every option to `effect/cli`, so `--help` lists each one and `effect/cli` validates its value.
The command takes the order of steps from the raw tokens after `link`, not from `effect/cli`'s parsed result.
Before printing, the command checks that each section ID is a heading in `prd.md` or `spec.md`.
Before printing, the command checks that each task is in the manifest.
Before printing, the command checks that a commit is known to git and, when it follows a task, carries that task's `Cairn-Task` trailer.
Before printing, the command checks that a stack or segment root has `parent: null`.
Before printing, the command checks that a task followed by `--file` has commits.
Before printing, the command checks that the steps are well formed.
A failed check exits with code 1 and a message naming the bad token, such as `unknown section prd.code-veiw`, `t74 has no commits, so it has no diff yet` or `--line must follow --file`.
The command does not check that a passage, a file or a line still exists. The viewer reports any that are missing.
The printed link is `http://localhost:4310`, the port `cairn serve` uses, followed by the path.
`--base <url>` sets a different origin for the printed link, and `--base ""` prints the path alone.
The command reads files and git but never writes anything.

`AGENTS.md` says that a pull request description, a gate notice and a board post name the place they are about with `cairn link`, and gives the `cairn link prd.code-view t74 --file packages/cli/src/api.ts --line 40` example.
The `detail` of a `blocked_on_human` event from the orchestrator ends with `cairn link <task>`.
A pull request opened by `gt submit` links its task and the task's first PRD section.
Once there is a message board adapter, board posts name their place with `cairn link` too.

decisions.why: It is the port `cairn serve` uses.

decisions.text: `--file` after a task first inserts a `diff` step at the task's newest commit.

sections.title: Reference from code
sections.summary: Builds a build-time generator that writes the CLI reference pages from the `effect/cli` command definitions and the `.cairn/` file pages from the contract's generated JSON Schema. It also adds a check that fails the build when a docs page names a `cairn` command that no longer exists.

requirements.text: `packages/cli/src/commands/index.ts` exports `commands`, the list of `effect/cli` command definitions that `main.ts` composes.
`reference.ts` runs at build time and writes reference pages that are not committed to the repository.
`reference.ts` writes one CLI page per command, holding its usage line, its description, its options with their types and defaults, and its subcommands.

`reference.ts` writes one page per file in `.cairn/`. Pages for the JSON files come from the contract's generated JSON Schema and list each field's name, type, whether it is required, its default and its description annotation.
The JSON file pages cover the `judgments`, `spec-index` and `trace` schemas that the generation in `spec.contract.javascript-entry` adds.
A schema field with no description shows `—` in its page's table.
When a schema field has no description, the build prints a warning that names the field.
The pages for `prd.md`, `spec.md` and `cairn.db` are written by hand, not generated.

`check-pages.ts` fails the build when a page names a command in backticks (`` `cairn <word>` ``) that `commands` does not contain. The error gives the file and line, for example `getting-started.md:12 names cairn foo, which no longer exists`.

`apps/viewer/package.json` exports `./markdown`, `./search` and the viewer's `ui` stylesheets for use by the docs app.

Built docs assets go where the installed Alchemy's `Cloudflare.Website` takes built assets.

sections.title: Agent access
sections.summary: Builds agent access to Cairn: the CLI and a stdio MCP server (`cairn mcp`) as thin adapters over one shared operation layer in `packages/cli/src/operations/`, with schemas in `@cairn/contract`. Planning's questions and reviews become resumable decisions, and the work includes a guide and setup instructions.

requirements.text: An agent can use Cairn through either the CLI or the `cairn mcp` MCP server.
The CLI and the MCP server are both thin adapters over one shared set of operations in `packages/cli/src/operations/`.
Each operation's input, output and error schemas are defined in `@cairn/contract`.
A CLI command turns its arguments into an operation's input and prints the operation's result.
An MCP tool decodes its JSON arguments with the same operation input schema the CLI uses and returns the encoded result.
Neither the CLI adapter nor the MCP adapter builds a shell command.
Neither the CLI adapter nor the MCP adapter parses terminal output.
Validation, file writes, redaction and gate rules live in the operation, not in either adapter.
Agent access through the CLI or MCP server must not require a room or multiplayer.
Planning's questions and reviews are exposed as decisions that can be resumed.
The MCP server runs over stdio.
MCP tools are provided for the commands that ship later, not only for the commands that exist before the operation layer.
A guide and setup instructions for agent access are provided.

sections.title: Operations
sections.summary: Declares Cairn's operations as data in the contract package (Operation, OperationError, Finding, humanOnly) and adds the init, ids, lint and status operations. Both adapters run them through a single runOperation entry point. Writes are atomic and recorded, an operations table logs each run so interrupted runs are reported, and an equivalence test checks that the CLI and JSON paths give the same results.

requirements.text: `packages/contract/src/operations.ts` declares each operation as data and imports IDs from `ids.ts`. `packages/contract/src/index.ts` re-exports it.
An operation's `name` is a slug that serves as the MCP tool name, with "-" written as "_". Its `command` is the CLI form of the same operation.
The `Finding` type moves from core's `lint.ts` to `operations.ts`, and core's `lint.ts` imports it from there.
`humanOnly` in `operations.ts` lists the commands that are never operations. It holds `approve`.
The `init` operation takes `{}`, returns `{ created: Array<string> }` and has the effect `local-write`.
The `ids` operation takes `{ check: boolean }`, returns `{ added: Array<{ file, id, line }>; missing: number }` and has the effect `local-write`.
The `lint` operation takes `{}`, returns `{ findings: Array<Finding>; errors: number; warnings: number }` and has the effect `read`.
The `status` operation takes `{ task: TaskId | null }`, returns `{ trace: Trace; needsHuman: Array<{ task: TaskId; reasons: Array<GateReason>; action: string }> }` and has the effect `read`.
`ids` with `check: true` writes nothing, but the operation still declares the `local-write` effect.
Lint findings are returned as a result, not as an error. The `cairn lint` CLI still exits 1 when `errors > 0`.
The `status` operation leaves out the private trace fields, as `cairn status --json` does without `--private`.
The `status` operation must not refresh the manifest snapshot itself. That stays the `cairn status` command's own step.
`needsHuman` lists each `blocked_on_human` task. Its `action` says what a person does, such as `A person reviews t12 and runs cairn approve t12.`.
No operation appends an event.
`runOperation(op, rawInput)` in `packages/cli/src/operations/run.ts` is the only entry point that both adapters call.
`runOperation` decodes the input with `op.input`. A decode failure is an `invalid-input` error carrying the field path.
For every operation except `init`, `runOperation` checks that `.cairn/` exists. If it does not, it fails with `not-initialized` and the hint `Call init first.`.
`runOperation` runs the operation with an `OperationContext` service. Its `progress(message, done?, total?)` reports progress, and its `WriteLog` records what was written.
`errorOf` maps every typed error the commands already raise to an `OperationError`. Each error gets one code, the existing message becomes `message`, and a defect becomes `internal`.
Every file an operation writes goes through `writeFileAtomic(path, bytes)`. It writes a temporary file in the same directory, renames it into place and then records the path in the `WriteLog`.
The init, ids, lint and status commands must not write through `FileSystem` directly.
An operation that fails or is interrupted reports, in `OperationError.changed`, exactly the files it had already replaced, relative to the repo root.
A new migration adds the table `operations(id text primary key, name text, started_at text, ended_at text, outcome text, changed text)`.
`runOperation` writes an `operations` row when an operation starts and closes it with the outcome `ok`, `failed` or `interrupted`. When the process dies, the row stays open.

On the next `status` call from either interface, every `operations` row that is open or `interrupted` and has not been reported yet becomes an `interrupted-operation` warning that names its files. The row is then marked as reported.
`init` writes its `operations` row once `cairn.db` exists.
The commands `cairn init`, `cairn ids`, `cairn lint` and `cairn status` become adapters. Each one parses its options, calls `runOperation` and prints the result as it prints today.
In the CLI, an `OperationError` prints to stderr as `error <code>: <message>`, followed by the hint, and the process exits 1.

sections.title: Review checkpoints
sections.summary: Turns `cairn plan` into a `plan` operation that stops at each review question (statements, spec, tasks) and returns it as a stored, revision-guarded decision, plus a `plan-continue` operation that applies the answer. The interactive CLI and new `--json` and `--continue` flags drive the same two operations.

requirements.text: `plan` is an operation that stops at each question it would ask the person and returns that question as a decision (`PlanResult` of kind `needs-decision`).
A second operation, `plan-continue`, applies the answer to a decision returned by `plan`.
The interactive CLI calls the same `plan` and `plan-continue` operations and answers in process, so it behaves as it does today.
`plan` has no `yes` field: `--yes` stays a CLI flag that a person types, and no tool can set it.

A decision's `continueWith` tells the agent what to do next in both the tool form and the CLI form, e.g. `Ask the person, then call plan_continue with decision d_k2m9x1 (CLI: cairn plan --continue d_k2m9x1 --answer yes).`
An empty `part` in `PlanInput` plans the whole PRD.
A decision ID matches `^d_[a-z0-9]{6,}$`.
In `ContinueInput.answers` for a statements decision, a draft left out is skipped.
A new migration adds the table `plan_decisions(id text primary key, checkpoint text, revision text, payload text, created_at text, used_at text)`.

A decision's payload holds what continuing needs: the run's input, and at the tasks checkpoint the drafted and judged tasks, the split sections and the judgments, so that a yes writes exactly what was reviewed and never drafts again.

A decision's revision is the SHA-256 of the bytes of `prd.md`, `spec.md`, `spec.json`, `manifest.json` and `judgments.json`, plus the payload's hash, as they stood when the decision was returned; a missing file counts as empty.

`plan-continue` recomputes the revision from the files on disk and, when it differs, fails with `stale-decision`, naming the files that changed, with the hint `Call plan again; it continues from the files as they are.`
`plan-continue` on a decision that was already used fails with `decision-used`.
`plan-continue` on an unknown decision fails with `unknown-decision`.
At the statements checkpoint, the answers go through `settle`, then the spec step runs, as `spec.planning.cairn-plan` does at that point.
A yes to the spec decision drafts the tasks, which leads to the tasks decision.
A no to the spec decision returns `stopped` with the message the CLI prints.
A yes to the tasks decision writes the manifest, the spec, `spec.json` and `judgments.json` in the existing order, and lint errors refuse the write as before.
A no to the tasks decision returns `stopped`.
`stopAfter: "spec"` returns `stopped` after the spec is written and makes no spec decision.
`dryRun` returns `dry-run` and makes no decision.
`plan-accept`, with input `{ section: SpecSectionId }`, is `cairn plan --accept` as an operation.
Planning never touches a gate: no planning step appends to `events.jsonl`, so a decision cannot approve anything.
`cairn plan --json` runs `plan`, prints the `PlanResult` as JSON and exits 0, whether or not it returned a decision.
`cairn plan --continue <decision>` takes `--answer yes|no` or `--answers <file.json>`, where the file holds the `answers` object.
The interactive `cairn plan` loops: it calls `plan`, asks each question on the terminal, calls `plan-continue`, and repeats until the result is not a decision, with its prompts and output unchanged.
`--yes` makes the interactive loop answer `yes` to the spec and tasks decisions and skip every draft.

tests.text: With the scripted Planner and Judge in a temporary repository, `plan` on a PRD with drafts returns a statements decision; continuing it returns a spec decision and then a tasks decision; a yes writes a manifest that is field for field the reviewed `review.new`.
Editing `spec.md` after the spec decision makes `plan-continue` fail with `stale-decision`, naming `.cairn/spec.md`, and nothing is written.
Using a decision twice fails with `decision-used`.
After the whole flow, `events.jsonl` is byte for byte unchanged, and a gated task is still `blocked_on_human` or `pending` as before.
The equivalence harness runs the flow through the CLI (`--json` and `--continue`) and the JSON leg on the same fixture, and gets the same `.cairn/` files and the same `stale-decision` failure.
The interactive `cairn plan` tests in `spec.planning.cairn-plan` pass unchanged.

decisions.text: `plan` stops at each question and returns it as a decision, with a separate `plan-continue` operation that applies the answer, instead of prompting on the terminal.
decisions.why: An agent has no terminal prompt to answer.

decisions.text: The interactive CLI calls the same two operations and answers in process rather than keeping a separate code path.
decisions.why: So it behaves as it does today.

decisions.text: `plan` has no `yes` field; `--yes` stays a CLI flag that a person types and no tool can set.
The decision payload stores the run's input and, at the tasks checkpoint, the drafted and judged tasks, split sections and judgments.
decisions.why: So a yes writes exactly what was reviewed and never drafts again.

decisions.text: The revision hashes the bytes of the planning files plus the payload's hash, and `plan-continue` refuses with `stale-decision` when it differs.
decisions.why: This covers a person editing the spec between the review and the answer.

decisions.text: A missing file counts as empty when computing the revision.
Planning never touches a gate and no step appends to `events.jsonl`.
decisions.why: So a decision cannot approve anything.

decisions.text: `cairn plan --json` exits 0 whether or not it returned a decision.

sections.title: MCP server
sections.summary: Builds `cairn mcp`, an MCP server over stdio bound to one repository, which advertises Cairn's existing operations as tools from a registry, runs calls through `runOperation` with progress and cancellation, and keeps stdout for protocol messages only. It also adds an MCP leg to the equivalence harness and end-to-end, cancellation and shutdown tests.

requirements.text: `cairn mcp [--repo <path>]` starts an MCP server over stdio for one repository.
Before the server is written, the declarations of the installed `effect` for `McpServer` in `effect/unstable/ai` are read to check for a stdio layer, progress notifications and request cancellation.
If effect's `McpServer` has a stdio layer, progress notifications and request cancellation, the server uses it and Cairn adds no dependency.
If effect's `McpServer` lacks any of a stdio layer, progress notifications or request cancellation, the server uses `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` at the version current that day, pinned exactly.
The tests use the MCP SDK's `Client` with `StdioClientTransport`, as a dev dependency, whichever library the server uses.
At startup `cairn mcp` resolves the repository from `--repo`, or else from the working directory.
`cairn mcp` finds the main checkout the same way every other command does.
When the resolved directory is outside a git repository, `cairn mcp` exits 1 with a message on stderr before any protocol message is sent.
The server starts even when `.cairn/` does not exist yet; the `init` tool creates it, and other tools return `not-initialized` until it does.
No tool input names a repository or a path to open, so a call cannot point the server at another location.
File paths inside tool inputs, such as a link's file, are repo-relative strings that are validated and never opened.
The server's stdout carries protocol messages only.
The composition root replaces Effect's logger with one that writes to stderr.
`console.log`, `console.info` and `console.debug` are pointed at stderr before anything else runs.
Tools come from a registry in `tools.ts` that is a list of operations.
Each tool's name is the operation's name with `-` written as `_`.

Each tool's description ends with one sentence for each of the operation's effects: "Reads only.", "Writes files in .cairn/.", "Calls a model, which can cost money or subscription allowance." or "Writes outside this machine.".
Each tool's `inputSchema` and `outputSchema` are generated from the operation's contract schemas with `Schema.toJsonSchemaDocument`.
A tool carries the `readOnlyHint` annotation when its operation's effects are only `read`.
A tool carries the `openWorldHint` annotation when its operation has the `model-cost` or `external-write` effect.
Every tool carries the annotation `destructiveHint: false`.
`read` operations and `ids` carry the `idempotentHint` annotation.
Each tool has `_meta` holding `cairn/effects` and `cairn/command`.
Tool metadata only describes the operation; `runOperation` enforces the operation's rules.
A command that only starts a transport or a terminal (`mcp`, `watch`, `serve` as a blocking process) is not exposed as a tool.
Nothing in `humanOnly` is exposed as a tool.
The registry holds only operations that exist, so a command still to be built is never advertised.
A tool call runs `runOperation`; on success it returns `structuredContent` with the encoded output and one text block with a short summary for clients that do not read structured content.
An `OperationError` from a tool call returns `isError: true`, with the error as `structuredContent` and the error's message and hint as text.
Operations with the `local-write` effect run one at a time, behind a semaphore.
Read operations run concurrently.
When a request carries a `progressToken`, each `OperationContext.progress` call becomes a `notifications/progress` message.
In the CLI, each `OperationContext.progress` call is written as a line on stderr.
`notifications/cancelled` interrupts the operation's fiber, and the fiber's scope ends the planner's child processes.
A cancelled call returns `cancelled` with `changed` taken from the `WriteLog`, and the operation log records the cancellation.
When stdin closes, or on SIGTERM or SIGINT, the server closes its root scope, interrupting every running operation, and the operation log records the interruptions for the next `status`.
On shutdown the server stops anything it started and exits 0.

tests.text: The equivalence harness gains a third leg that starts `cairn mcp` as a child process and sends each fixture case as a `tools/call` through the SDK client; the resulting `.cairn/` trees and error codes equal the CLI leg's.

End-to-end in a fresh git repository with a stub `claude` on a temporary PATH answering from fixtures/stub-claude/, using only MCP requests: tools/list returns exactly the registry's tools with schemas and effects; init creates .cairn/ and the test writes a PRD; ids assigns its IDs; plan returns a statements decision and plan_continue returns the spec then tasks decisions; plan_continue with yes writes the manifest; lint and status read the result.
`tools/list` holds no `approve` tool, and no sequence of calls in the end-to-end run appends to `events.jsonl`.
Every line the server writes to stdout during the end-to-end run decodes as a JSON-RPC message while operations log at debug level.
A `plan` call against a stub `claude` that sleeps is cancelled; the result is `cancelled` and no process with the stub's marker argument is left running.
A run that closes stdin mid-call: the server exits, no stub process remains, and the next `status` reports the interrupted operation with its files.

decisions.text: Use effect's own `McpServer` when it has a stdio layer, progress notifications and request cancellation; otherwise use `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` pinned exactly at the then-current version.
decisions.why: Using effect's server means Cairn adds no dependency.

decisions.text: The server is bound to one repository at startup, and no tool input names a repository or a path to open; paths in inputs are validated repo-relative strings that are never opened.
decisions.why: So a call cannot point the server anywhere else.

decisions.text: The server does not require `.cairn/` to exist at startup; `init` creates it and other tools return `not-initialized` until then.
Tool metadata only describes an operation; enforcement stays in `runOperation`.
Commands that only start a transport or terminal (`mcp`, `watch`, blocking `serve`) and anything in `humanOnly` are left out of the tools.
The registry lists only operations that exist.
decisions.why: So a command still to be built is never advertised.

decisions.text: `local-write` operations are serialized behind a semaphore while reads run concurrently.

sections.title: More tools
sections.summary: Adds an operation and a matching MCP tool for `judge`, `stats`, `link`, `note add`, `note resolve` and starting and stopping `serve`, each a small adapter over the existing operation layer. It also says which commands get no tool.

requirements.text: `cairn judge` gets a `judge` operation and MCP tool with input `{ fresh: boolean; strict: boolean }`, output `{ judgments: Array<Judgment>; flags: number }`, and effects `local-write` and `model-cost`.
`cairn stats --json` gets a `stats` operation and MCP tool with input `{ category: string | null; since: string | null }`, output the `--json` shape of `spec.status.cairn-stats`, and effect `read`.
`cairn link` gets a `link` operation and MCP tool with input `{ steps: Array<LinkArg>; base: string | null }`, output `{ path: string; url: string }`, and effect `read`.
`cairn note add` gets a `note-add` operation and MCP tool with input `{ kind; author; session; body; anchor: Array<LinkArg> }`, output `{ id: NoteId; link: string }`, and effect `local-write`.
`cairn note resolve` gets a `note-resolve` operation and MCP tool with input `{ id: NoteId }`, output `{ id: NoteId }`, and effect `local-write`.
`cairn serve` gets a `serve-start` operation and MCP tool with input `{}`, output `{ url: string; alreadyRunning: boolean }`, and effect `read`.
Stopping `cairn serve` gets a `serve-stop` operation and MCP tool with input `{}`, output `{ stopped: boolean }`, and effect `read`.
`judge` called with `strict: true` when flags are present returns the `judge-flagged` error, which is the error the CLI's exit code 1 stands for.

`LinkArg` is the structured form of a `cairn link` token. It is one of `{ section }`, `{ passage: { section, text } }`, `{ task }`, `{ commit }`, `{ file }`, `{ lines: { start, end, old } }`, `{ stack }`, `{ segment }`, `{ turn }` or `{ note }`.
The `link` operation turns its `LinkArg` list into tokens and runs `stepsOfArgs`, so the CLI and the MCP tool validate the same way and fail with the same messages.
`serve-start` runs the server layer of `serve.ts` in a fiber forked into the MCP server's root scope.
`serve-start` returns once the port is listening and does not hold the call open.
A second `serve-start` call while the server is running returns the same URL with `alreadyRunning: true`.
`serve-start` fails with `port-in-use` when the port is taken.
`serve-stop` interrupts the server fiber.
Closing the MCP server also stops a server started by `serve-start`.
The CLI's `cairn serve` still blocks until Ctrl-C. The CLI does not start `serve-start` or `serve-stop` through `runOperation`, but it uses the same server layer they do.
`cairn judge --compare` must not be exposed as an MCP tool.
The `cairn session` commands must not be exposed as MCP tools.
`approve` must not be exposed as an MCP tool. It stays human-only.

sections.title: Agent guide
sections.summary: Writes the agent guide: a short `SKILL.md` shipped with the CLI package and a matching docs page, `10-agents.md`. Together they cover the workflow, the human checkpoints, how to recover from each error, the limits and MCP setup. The page also includes a tools table that `reference.ts` generates from the registry.

requirements.text: `SKILL.md` is a short skill whose frontmatter has a `name` and a `description`.
`SKILL.md` is shipped in the CLI package's files.
`SKILL.md` covers the workflow in both CLI and MCP form: init, the person edits `prd.md`, ids, plan, then lint and status.
`SKILL.md` tells the agent to pass every statement draft and both reviews on to the person, along with what the result's `review` holds.
`SKILL.md` tells the agent never to answer for the person.
`SKILL.md` tells the agent never to pass `--yes` unless the person says to.
`SKILL.md` says that a gate is approved by a person running `cairn approve`, never by the agent.

`SKILL.md` gives a recovery step for each error code an operation returns, such as `not-initialized` (run init), `stale-decision` (plan again) and `cancelled` (read `changed`). It also says how to recover from lint findings.
`SKILL.md` states the limits: one repository per server, stdio only, and no remote access yet.
`apps/docs/pages/10-agents.md` says the same as `SKILL.md` in the docs.
The agents page gives the setup command `claude mcp add cairn -- cairn mcp --repo <path>`.
The agents page gives the generic JSON entry for a client's MCP config, with `command: "cairn"` and `args: ["mcp", "--repo", "<path>"]`.
The agents page says that people and agents with a shell need no MCP client.
`reference.ts` writes `agents/tools.md` from the registry, with one row per tool giving the tool, its CLI command, its effects and its description.
The agents page includes the generated `agents/tools.md` table.

sections.title: Terminal view
sections.summary: Builds `cairn watch`, a read-only terminal viewer that follows `.cairn/` and git, rebuilds the trace into a Model and draws it with a pure `view` into a Frame. The section covers the refresh pipeline and the screen layout: a top status line, a task tree pane, a detail pane for the selected task and a key-hint line.

requirements.text: `cairn watch` follows the `.cairn/` files and git, and keeps the current trace in a Schema-defined Model.
`cairn watch` draws the Model with a pure `view` function into a Frame, and a Screen writes that Frame to the terminal.
`cairn watch` must not write anything. It only reads, so closing it or crashing it has no effect on the run.
Any number of terminals and browsers may watch one repository at the same time.
A refresh is triggered both by file watchers on `.cairn/` and git and by a poll every 2 seconds.
Refresh triggers are debounced by 100 ms.
When the input hash has not changed since the last build, the refresh is skipped and the trace is not rebuilt.
The trace is built with `buildTrace`, the same way `cairn status --json` builds it, and passed to `update` as a `ReceivedTrace` message.
The Screen writes only the cells that changed in the Frame.
The top line shows the feature, the count of tasks in each status, the cost so far and the time since the first event.
The cost on the top line is the sum of known billed cost. When some attempts have no cost, it is followed by `+N unknown`, where N is the number of those attempts.
The elapsed time on the top line runs from the earliest event's `ts` to the Model's `now`.
The left pane starts with a "Waiting on a human" block that lists every task in `blocked_on_human` status.
After the waiting block, the left pane shows the stacks as a tree in `cairn status` order. Each row has the task's status symbol, ID, title and gate marker.
For the selected task, the right pane shows its PRD and spec sections, branch and worktree.
For the selected task, the right pane shows what the task ran on beside what the plan chose.
For the selected task, the right pane shows its attempts, each with its usage and cost.
For the selected task, the right pane shows its events in order, its gate reasons, and its commits with their session IDs.
For the selected task, the right pane shows its viewer link exactly as `cairn link <task>` prints it.
The bottom line shows the keys that apply in the current state.
At a terminal width of 100 columns or more, both panes show, and the tree pane takes `max(36, 45%)` of the width.

sections.title: Rendering library
sections.summary: Builds the CLI watch view's rendering layer: a spike that tests OpenTUI's core against four requirements, a pure in-memory Frame model in frame.ts, and a Screen service with a memory implementation for tests and a diffing ANSI implementation. The ANSI screen has no dependencies and is the fallback if the spike fails.

requirements.text: Before the screen is built, a spike must check OpenTUI's framework-independent core against four requirements.
The spike must check that OpenTUI's core runs on every Node version in packages/cli/package.json's engines with no experimental flag.

The spike must check that OpenTUI's core installs from npm with no build step on macOS, Linux and Windows. It must read this from the published platform packages and confirm it with an install on each system.
The spike must check that OpenTUI's core needs no UI framework.
The spike must check that OpenTUI's core can render to memory.
SPIKE.md must record the answer to each spike requirement with its source and date.
If all four spike requirements pass, screen.ts must get an OpenTUI-backed implementation.
If any spike requirement fails, the screen must be plain ANSI with no dependency.
Terminal Kit may be used only if the spike finds that keys or resize do not work in Windows Terminal without it.
frame.ts must be pure and independent of the rendering library.
put must clip text to the given width, and clipped text must end in "…" or "...".
Text must be split into graphemes with Intl.Segmenter, and each grapheme must take exactly one column.
Clipping must keep a row inside its pane, even when a wide character shifts the rest of the row.
MemoryScreen must keep the last frame drawn, for tests.
On entering, AnsiScreen must switch to the alternate screen (\x1b[?1049h) and hide the cursor.
When AnsiScreen draws, it must compare the new frame with the last one and write cursor moves, SGR codes and characters only for runs of cells that changed.
When the frame size changes, AnsiScreen must redraw everything.
With colour off, AnsiScreen must write no foreground colour codes but must still write bold, dim and inverse.
AnsiScreen's leave must reset SGR, show the cursor and return to the main screen (\x1b[?1049l).

sections.title: Trace stream
sections.summary: Builds `traceStream(root)`, a scoped stream that watches `.cairn/` and git refs and also polls. After a debounce it rebuilds the trace through the same `buildTrace` the `/api/trace` route uses, but only when the input hash has changed.

requirements.text: `traceStream(root)` is a scoped `Stream<Either<Trace, TraceLoadError>>`.
`api.ts` exposes `traceInputsHash(root)`, the hash behind the `/api/trace` `ETag`, and `buildTrace(root)`, and `traceStream` uses both.
`cairn status --json` still builds its trace through the same `buildTrace`.
The stream is triggered by a `FileSystem.watch` on `.cairn/`.
The stream is triggered by a `FileSystem.watch` on the git common directory's `refs/`, `packed-refs` and `HEAD`.
The stream is triggered by a poll every two seconds.
A watcher that fails is re-armed every second, and the poll keeps running in the meantime.
Triggers are debounced by 100 ms.
After the debounce the input hash is read, and the trace is built and emitted only when that hash differs from the last one emitted, so a burst of events gives one build.
A build that fails emits the error, and the next trigger tries the build again.
The stream keeps the last emitted hash as its only state.
Every build reads the trace again from the files, and derivation recomputes it from scratch.
The stream never writes. Unlike the `cairn status` command, it does not refresh the manifest snapshot.
Closing the stream's scope leaves no watcher open.

sections.title: Model, update and view
sections.summary: Builds the terminal watch view in the same shape as the viewer: a Schema-defined WatchModel, fact-named Messages, a single `update` returning commands and a single `view` producing a Frame, plus a symbol table for statuses in Unicode and ASCII. It also sets out the memory, selection, tick and layout rules, and the tests for them.

requirements.text: The terminal view is built the way the viewer is: a Schema-defined Model, fact-named Messages, one `update` function and one `view` function.
Only `view` knows the terminal exists, and only as far as the `Frame` type goes.
The WatchModel holds the current trace and must not hold anything gathered over the run.
The selected task's events are read from the current trace when `view` runs, so memory follows the size of the trace and not how many times it changed.
A `ReceivedTrace` message replaces the trace held in the model.
The selection is held by row key (for example "waiting:t12" or "tree:t12").
When the selected row is gone or filtered out after a new trace arrives, the selection moves to the row now at the selected row's old index, or to the last row.
A `Ticked` message arrives once a second, and only the time on the top line changes in response.
Rows come from `statusTreeOf`, counts from `statusCountsOf`, statuses from the trace's derived status, and what ran from `ranOf`.
`view` must not compute rows, counts, statuses or what ran itself.
`symbols.ts` maps each status to a symbol and a word in two sets: Unicode (`○ ◐ ⚑ ✕ ✓ ⇡`, with `├─ └─` for the tree) and ASCII (`o ~ ! x v ^`, with `|- \-` for the tree).
The gate marker is `⚑` in the Unicode set and `G!` in the ASCII set.
A status is always drawn as its symbol, and in the detail pane as its word as well.
Colour is only ever added beside a status's symbol and word, never in place of them, so colour never carries information alone.
In the narrow layout the tree fills the width, and the task screen replaces the tree instead of sitting beside it.

`view` takes rows, counts, statuses and what ran from the shared core functions (`statusTreeOf`, `statusCountsOf`, derived status, `ranOf`) and computes none of them itself.

sections.title: Keys
sections.summary: Defines the terminal view's key handling: the `Key` type, a pure `keysFor(model)` that lists the keys that apply now (drawn on the bottom line), and how `update` acts on each key. That covers navigation, opening a task, text and status filtering, help, opening the task in the viewer and quitting.

requirements.text: `keysFor(model)` must be pure and return the keys that apply in the current model, each with its label.
The bottom line of the terminal view must draw the list of keys returned by `keysFor(model)`.
`update` must handle a key only when it is in the `keysFor` list. Otherwise it returns the model unchanged with no command, so a key that is not shown does nothing.
Up, Down, `j` and `k` apply when there are rows or the task screen is open. They move the selection, and in the task screen they scroll the detail.
Enter applies when a row is selected and the filter is not being edited. It opens the selected task full width, as the narrow layout does.
Escape applies when the task screen is open, filter text is set or help is shown. It goes back to the tree if the task screen is open, otherwise clears the filter, otherwise closes help.
`/` applies when not editing and starts editing the filter.
While editing the filter, any character and Backspace edit the filter as it is typed.
While editing the filter, Enter stops editing and keeps the filter text.
While editing the filter, Escape clears the filter.
`f` applies when not editing. It cycles the status filter through all, then each status in contract order, then back to all.
`o` applies when a task is selected and the filter is not being edited. It sends `CheckServe` for `http://localhost:4310`.
`?` applies when not editing and toggles the key list.
`q` applies when not editing and sends `Quit`.
Ctrl-C always applies and sends `Quit`.
While editing the filter, `j`, `k`, `q`, `f` and `o` are treated as filter text, not as commands.
While editing the filter, Up and Down still move the selection.
The text filter keeps a row when its task ID, its title or any of its PRD or spec section IDs contains the filter text as a plain substring, ignoring case.
The status filter is applied on top of the text filter.
`CheckServe` requests `/api/trace` with a 300 ms timeout.
When the server answers, `CheckedServe` sends `OpenUrl` with `http://localhost:4310` plus `LinkFromPath` of `[{ kind: "task", id }]` for the selected task.
`OpenUrl` runs `open`, `xdg-open` or `cmd /c start "" <url>`, passing the URL as an argument list.
After opening a task in the viewer, the notice reads `Opened <task id> in the viewer`, for example `Opened t12 in the viewer`.
When the server does not answer `CheckServe`, the notice shows the link instead.

sections.title: `cairn watch`
sections.summary: Builds the `cairn watch` command: it refuses to run without a terminal, otherwise sets up colour/Unicode detection, raw mode, the alternate screen, listeners, signal handlers, the trace stream and a tick inside one Effect Scope, runs the update/view loop, and restores the terminal on every exit path. It runs on a read-only FileSystem, so it cannot affect the run it watches.

requirements.text: `cairn watch` must check for a terminal first, then run its loop inside one Scope.
When `process.stdout.isTTY` or `process.stdin.isTTY` is false, `cairn watch` must not write anything to stdout.
When stdout or stdin is not a TTY, `cairn watch` must write `cairn watch needs a terminal. For scripts, run cairn status --json.` to stderr and exit with code 1.
`cairn watch` must never prompt when it is not running in a terminal.
Colour must be on unless `NO_COLOR` is set to a non-empty value or `stdout.hasColors()` returns false.
Unicode must be on when the first of `LC_ALL`, `LC_CTYPE` or `LANG` that is set names UTF-8 (case-insensitive), or when `WT_SESSION` is set on Windows; otherwise the view must use the ASCII symbols.
Raw mode must be acquired with `Effect.acquireRelease` in the command's Scope, together with `readline.emitKeypressEvents`, and its keypress listener must send a `PressedKey` message.
The `AnsiScreen` must be entered and left through `Effect.acquireRelease` in the command's Scope.
A `resize` listener that sends a `Resized` message must be acquired with `Effect.acquireRelease` in the command's Scope.
Handlers for SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGHUP that interrupt the main fiber must be acquired with `Effect.acquireRelease` in the command's Scope.
The trace stream's fibers and watchers must be acquired with `Effect.acquireRelease` in the command's Scope.
A one-second tick must be acquired with `Effect.acquireRelease` in the command's Scope.
The loop must fold Messages through `update`, run the resulting Commands, and draw `view` after each batch, at most once per 16 ms animation tick.

`Quit` must end the main fiber, after which the Scope closes in reverse order: leaving the alternate screen, showing the cursor, turning raw mode off, removing the listeners and stopping the watchers.
On a defect, the command must close the Scope first and only then print the defect to stderr and exit with code 1.
A `process.once("exit")` handler must write the terminal restore sequence synchronously when the Scope never finished closing.
The command's composition root must provide the `FileSystem` from `read-only.ts`, which fails with a defect on any write.
The command's composition root must not provide a `TraceStore` that writes.
`cairn watch` must not write anything that the orchestrator or derivation reads, so a failure in the view can only stop the view and never affects the run.

sections.title: `cairn doctor`
sections.summary: Builds the read-only `cairn doctor` command, which runs three checks in order (git, config, planner), prints one plain `ok`/`fail` line per check saying what to fix, and exits 0 only when every check passes.

requirements.text: `cairn doctor` must not write any file.
`cairn doctor` must not make any network request.
`cairn doctor` must not call a model or build a model Layer.
`cairn doctor` runs three checks in order, git, then config, then planner, and each check prints exactly one line.
A passing line starts with `ok`, followed by the check name and a message.
A failing line starts with `fail` and ends with what the user should run or set to fix it.
The command exits 0 when every line passes and 1 when any line fails.
Output lines are plain text with no colour; the words `ok` and `fail` carry the result.
Each check catches its own errors and turns them into a failing result, so one failing check never stops the checks after it.
The git check runs `git --version` through `ChildProcess` with an argument list and a five-second timeout.
The git check then runs `git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir` to find the main checkout, the same way every command does.
When git is not found, the git line fails with `git was not found on PATH. Install git.`
When run outside a git repository, the git line fails with `Not in a git repository. Run git init, or run cairn doctor inside your repo.`
The config check looks for `.cairn/` in the main checkout, or in the current directory when outside a repository.
When there is no `.cairn/` directory, the config line fails with `No .cairn directory in <dir>. Run cairn init.`

The config check decodes `.cairn/config.json` through the contract's `Config`; on a decode failure it prints the typed error, which names the file and the field path, followed by `Fix .cairn/config.json.`
A missing `config.json` decodes to the defaults and the config line passes with `no config.json; using the defaults`.
The planner check uses the decoded config, and uses the defaults when there is no `.cairn/` directory.
When `config.json` does not decode, the planner line fails with `Cannot check the planner until .cairn/config.json decodes.`

For planner source `cli`, the planner check runs `<planner.cli> --version` with a five-second timeout, and a binary that cannot be started fails with the message `spec.models` gives (for example `claude was not found. Install Claude Code, or set planner.cli or planner.source in .cairn/config.json.`).
The planner check must not check that the planner CLI is signed in.
For planner source `api`, the key variable checked is `planner.keyEnv`, or else the provider's default from the table in `spec.models`.
For planner source `api`, when the key variable is unset or empty, the planner line fails, naming the variable.
For provider `openai-compatible` with no key, the planner line passes with `no key needed for openai-compatible`.
For planner source `api`, when `planner.gatewayTokenEnv` is set, the variable it names must be set too; otherwise the planner line fails, naming that variable.
Environment variables are read with `Config.Redacted`.
Variable values must never be printed or logged; a line names the variable only.
`cairn doctor` must not check the judge.
`commands/doctor.ts` runs the three checks, prints `formatChecks(results)`, then exits with `exitCodeOf(results)`.
`formatChecks` is pure and pads the check names into columns.
The doctor command is in the `commands` list in `commands/index.ts`, so the docs reference picks it up with no page edited.
`main.ts` runs `cairn doctor` without first requiring `.cairn/`.

Each doctor test runs in a temporary directory, with `PATH` holding only the directories the test chooses and the environment supplied by `ConfigProvider.fromMap`, so the real environment is never read.
The stub `claude` in `fixtures/stub-claude/` prints a version.

tests.text: In a git repository whose `.cairn/config.json` decodes and names the `cli` source with `claude`, with the stub `claude` on `PATH`, the output is one `ok` line each for git, config and planner, and the exit code is 0.
In a folder with no `.cairn/`, the config line fails and contains `Run cairn init`, and the exit code is non-zero.

With `planner.source: "api"`, `provider: "anthropic"`, a model, and no `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the environment, the planner line fails and names `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`; the git and config lines still print, and the exit code is non-zero.
With `planner.keyEnv: "MY_KEY"` and `MY_KEY` unset, the planner line fails naming `MY_KEY`.
With provider `openai-compatible` and no key, the planner line passes.
With `planner.gatewayTokenEnv` set to a variable that is unset, the planner line fails naming that variable.
A config with a bad field fails the config line naming the field, and the planner line says it cannot check until the config decodes.
With `planner.cli: "codex"` and no `codex` on `PATH`, the planner line gives the `spec.models` not-found message.
With `PATH` holding only the stub directory, the git line says git was not found, and the config and planner lines still print.
With a key set to a known value, the output does not contain that value.
Every file in the temporary directory is byte for byte the same after the run.

decisions.text: A missing `config.json` passes the config check, decoding to the defaults.
decisions.why: `cairn plan` runs with the defaults, so nothing needs fixing.

decisions.text: With no `.cairn/`, the planner check still runs using the default config.
decisions.why: So a fresh folder still learns whether its planner would work.

decisions.text: The planner check does not verify that the CLI is signed in.
decisions.why: That would take a model call.

decisions.text: Provider `openai-compatible` with no key passes the planner check.
decisions.why: A local endpoint takes no key.

decisions.text: The judge is not checked.
decisions.why: The PRD asks only about the planner, and `cairn plan` already says when judging is skipped.

decisions.text: The command exits 0 when every line passes and 1 when any fails.
decisions.why: So a script can run it first.

decisions.text: Unlike the other commands, `main.ts` runs `cairn doctor` without first requiring `.cairn/`.
`cairn doctor` is not an operation or an MCP tool in this section.

sections.title: Patch routes
sections.summary: Two git-backed routes on the dev server, GET /api/commits/:sha and GET /api/diffs/:base/:head, return a commit's patch and a task's whole diff as text for the code view.

requirements.text: `GET /api/commits/:sha` returns `git show --patch <sha>` as text.
`GET /api/diffs/:base/:head` returns `git diff --patch <base> <head>` as text.
Each SHA decodes through the contract's `Sha`; anything else is `400` and never reaches git.
Git runs as a child process with an argument list, never through a shell.
A SHA git does not know is `404`; any other git failure is `500` with git's message.
The body is `text/plain` with `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`.
In dev, Vite proxies `/api` to the server, as it proxies `/presence`.

tests.text: Against a temporary repository with two commits: the commit route returns the second commit's message and patch, the range route the change between them, and a malformed SHA, an unknown SHA and a range with an unknown end give 400, 404 and 404.

decisions.text: Ship the patch routes on the existing presence server before the rest of the API.
decisions.why: They need only git, so the code view can show real diffs before status derivation and the trace store exist.

sections.summary: Specifies the cairn serve HTTP and WebSocket routes on port 4310 and how the viewer polls them.

`GET /api/trace` returns the `Trace`, each spec section with its summary from `spec.json`, with an `ETag` from a hash of the inputs.
`GET /api/sessions/:id` returns the redacted session and its notes.
`GET /api/commits/:sha` returns `git show --patch` output as text, which `parsePatchFiles` reads.
`WS /presence` is unchanged.
`GET /*` serves the built viewer; in dev, Vite serves it and proxies `/api`.
The viewer polls `/api/trace` every two seconds with `If-None-Match`.
`Trace` is a contract schema (see spec.contract.trace) so the server encodes and the viewer decodes the same type.
A file watcher replaces polling later.
Each judgment in the Trace carries stale: boolean, true when its inputHash no longer matches the recomputed inputsOf.
`GET /api/diffs/:base/:head` returns a task's whole diff; both patch routes are specified in `spec.patch-routes`.

sections.title: Model and messages
sections.summary: Specifies the viewer model, the messages every screen shares, the pure chainOf function, hovering a chain, and the three-pane layout.

requirements.text: The model holds the trace, the screen, the reader's state, the hovered node, the detail panel's trail, the search, the presence state and the patches and sessions loaded so far.
`chainOf(trace, node)` is pure and returns the PRD sections, spec sections and tasks linked to a node, in both directions.
Hovering a spec card, a task row or a chip previews its chain: its curves are drawn in ink and every card, row and chip outside the chain is dimmed.
Layout is the PRD pane, the spec pane, then the stacks pane.
Each PRD heading carries its status line, and each task shows its status and a gate marker.
A spec card or task with a flag or unsure judgment shows a judgment marker, dimmed when the judgment is stale.
The stacks pane draws the plan's stack diagram, one box per stack in rows over the base branch, laid out by `stacksOf` (see spec.viewer.stacks).
Under cairn serve, a subscription in load.ts fetches /api/trace every two seconds with If-None-Match.
A 200 is decoded through the Trace schema and sends SettledLoadTrace with the trace; a 304 sends nothing.
A network or decode error sends SettledLoadTrace with the error, and the view shows the error above the last good trace.
The demo build (vite build --mode demo) loads demo-trace.json once and never polls.
A click does not pin a chain: a click on a task opens its detail, and the one thing a reader pins is a PRD section.

sections.title: Design system
sections.summary: Specifies the viewer's design tokens for a light and a dark palette, its three stylesheets, the classes and controls every view is built from, and the move of the code view to them.

requirements.text: Three stylesheets in `apps/viewer/src/ui/` are imported by `entry.ts` in order: `tokens.css` holds only custom properties on `:root`, `base.css` the page, the focus ring, prose and reduced motion, and `components.css` one class per piece.
Use Tailwind, CSS-in-JS or a preprocessor; a view applies a class with `h.Class` and keeps `h.Style` for a value that is computed.
The stylesheets select on the state attributes a view already sets, such as `aria-pressed`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-checked`, `aria-current`, `data-current` and `data-ran`.

Every colour is a token written once as `light-dark(<light>, <dark>)`; `:root` sets `color-scheme: light dark` and `index.html` a `color-scheme` meta tag, so the palette follows the system's setting with no switch, Model field or Message.
The palette is the section's table: the mockup's light values, with `--muted` one step darker and `--blocked-ink` added, and a dark value for each.
`--edge` and `--tint` are `color-mix()` of `--ink`, and text on any fill is `--ink`.

`light-only` sets `color-scheme: light` and the element's own colour and background again; highlighted code blocks, drawn diagrams and, until the canvas is removed, the canvas screen's `main` carry it.
Borders are `--line` (1.5px); radii are `--r-s` 4px, `--r-m` 8px and `--r-l` 12px; shadows are `--lift` and `--lift-l`, flat ink; a pressed button moves down 2px and loses its shadow.
Use a blurred shadow or a gradient.
The interface is `--mono` and prose is `--prose`, with no web font; sizes come from the eight `--t-*` tokens.
Motion uses `--ease` with `--d-fade` 150ms, `--d-press` 160ms and `--d-move` 240ms, animates only opacity, transform and colours, and is turned off under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.
Every button, link and divider shows `:focus-visible` as a 2px `--ink` outline, 2px off the element.
`components.css` has the classes of the section's table of pieces, and the views it names use them and write no rule of their own for them.
`marks.ts` exports `dotView`, `tagView`, `gateView` and `labelView`.

`switchView` is `Switch.view` from `@foldkit/ui` drawn as a `btn`, with `role="switch"` and `aria-checked`; `disclosureView` is `Disclosure.view`, giving `aria-expanded` and, while open, `aria-controls`, with the panel rendered only while open.
`segmentedView` is a labelled `role="group"` of native buttons with `aria-pressed`; it does not use `@foldkit/ui`'s `RadioGroup`.

The code view, the tree, the diff style control, search, the search mark, code blocks and diagrams move to the classes and lose their inline colours; the canvas's own views keep theirs until they are deleted.

sections.title: Reader
sections.summary: Specifies the reader screen: the PRD read as a document in its own pane, with a status line under each heading, and the section at the top of the pane, or the pinned one, as the current section the other panes follow.

requirements.text: The reader is a top bar over three panes, the PRD, the spec and the stacks; the window does not scroll and each pane has its own vertical scroll.
`Screen` gains `Reader`; until the canvas is removed the viewer opens on the canvas and "Plan" and "Canvas" buttons move between the two.
The model's `reader` holds only what a person has chosen: the section at the top, the pinned section, the density, the opened cards, whether models show, and the pane widths.
`currentOf` is the active search result's PRD section when there is one, else the pinned section, else the one at the top.
`sectionAtTop(tops, line)` is the last section whose top is at or above the line, or the first when none is; the level 1 heading is never current.
`cardsOf(trace, prd)` returns the spec sections of the chain in document order with their tasks in manifest order, and the strays: chain tasks no card lists.
`countsOf` gives the spec sections, tasks and done or landed tasks of a chain, and `planCountsOf` the same over every task.

Under each PRD heading a status line button shows the status word, the spec count and done/total tasks, and pins or unpins its section; a section with status deferred, context or unmapped shows a coverage note instead.
Each heading shows its section ID as a button that copies it through a Command.
A Mount on the PRD pane sends `ScrolledPrd` with the section at the top, at most once per animation frame and only when it changed; nothing else in the model changes on a scroll.
The spec pane's content is keyed by the current section so it starts at the top; the stacks pane keeps its scroll.
`PressedEscape` goes back one step in the detail panel when it is open, and otherwise unpins; the search control handles its own Escape first.
Read the Curves variant of the prototype for layout and spacing, and `spec.viewer.design-system` for colour, type, borders, shadows, motion and the classes and controls, before writing a view.

sections.title: Spec cards
sections.summary: Specifies the spec pane: one card per spec section that implements the current PRD section, with its summary, its tasks as rows inside it, and one control for how much of every card shows.

requirements.text: `specPaneView` draws `cardsOf(trace, current)` under a label and the density control.
A card is an article with `data-spec`: a header button from `disclosureView` with the title, done/total tasks and `aria-expanded`, the summary, and its task rows.
Run a stripe down a card's side; the header is a solid fill and the card has an ink border and a hard offset shadow.
A task row is a button with `data-task-row` of `<spec>:<task>` showing a status dot, ID, title, GATE, the model chip, and the commit count or the status word; it sends `ClickedTask`.
Task rows show at every density.
Strays are listed in a last card headed "Tasks that name this section directly", whose header is not a button.
A PRD section with a coverage note shows the note in place of the cards.
Density is titles, summary or full, summary at first, set by `segmentedView`'s three buttons with `aria-pressed`; `ClickedDensity` sets it and empties `opened`.

`renderSection(document, id, h, hooks)` renders the nodes from after a section's heading to the next heading of any level through the same code as `renderMarkdown`, without parsing the document again and keeping its block offsets.
